cases.question: Tell me about Mercury.
cases.reference_answer: 'Mercury' commonly refers to the planet (closest to the Sun), the chemical element Hg, or the Roman god.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the most likely sense (e.g. the planet) fully and cite it, then briefly note the other senses (element, Roman god).

answer.text:
"Mercury" is a famously ambiguous name — it most commonly refers to a planet, a chemical element, and a Roman god. Here is a summary of all three:

---

MERCURY THE PLANET

Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. It is a rocky world with a diameter of about 4,880 km (3,030 mi) and a surface that closely resembles Earth's Moon, covered in craters and vast plains. Its largest crater, Caloris Planitia, is about 1,550 km (960 mi) across — roughly one-third of the planet's diameter.

Because of a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, a single solar day (sunrise to sunrise) on Mercury lasts about 176 Earth days, even though a Mercurian year is only 88 Earth days long. Temperatures swing wildly as a result, ranging from -170 °C (-270 °F) at night to 420 °C (790 °F) in direct sunlight. Mercury has a very faint magnetic field and only a trace exosphere rather than a true atmosphere. Its permanently shadowed polar craters may contain water ice.

Mercury formed about 4.5 billion years ago and is thought to have had a magma ocean early in its history. It has been explored by the Mariner 10 flyby (1974) and the MESSENGER and BepiColombo orbiters. It is eventually expected to be destroyed when the Sun becomes a red giant in about seven to eight billion years.

---

MERCURY THE ELEMENT

Mercury the element has the chemical symbol Hg and atomic number 80. It is commonly called quicksilver and is the only metallic element that is liquid at standard room temperature and pressure. It is a heavy, silvery metal and occurs naturally in deposits around the world, mostly as the mineral cinnabar (mercuric sulfide). The red pigment vermilion is derived from cinnabar.

Mercury has historically been used in thermometers, barometers, and other instruments, as well as in fluorescent lamps and dental amalgam. However, it is highly toxic — exposure damages the nervous system, immune system, and kidneys — so its use in many everyday products has been significantly reduced over time.

---

MERCURY THE ROMAN GOD

In Roman religion, Mercury (Latin: Mercurius) was one of the 12 major gods of the ancient Roman pantheon. He was the god of boundaries, commerce, communication, eloquence, luck, travelers, and trickery, and served as the guide of souls to the underworld. He was the son of Jupiter and Maia (daughter of the Titan Atlas). Mercury is closely associated with the Greek god Hermes and is often depicted carrying the caduceus, a staff with intertwined snakes. The planet and the element were both named after him.

---

In short, "Mercury" is most likely to refer to the planet in everyday astronomical conversation, the element in a chemistry context, and the god in a mythology context. Let me know which you'd like to explore further!

Sources:
Mercury (planet) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet)
Mercury (element) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(element)
Mercury (mythology) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(mythology)

cases.question: If all roses are flowers and some flowers fade quickly, can we conclude that all roses fade quickly?
cases.reference_answer: No — that conclusion does not follow logically.
cases.expected_behavior: Answer the reasoning directly without searching; note it is not from Wikipedia.

answer.text:
This is a question of logical reasoning, not a factual lookup, so I can answer it directly without searching Wikipedia.

No, we cannot conclude that all roses fade quickly. Here is why:

The argument presented is a classic example of a logical fallacy known as the "undistributed middle" or an invalid syllogism. Let's break it down:

Premise 1: All roses are flowers. (Every rose belongs to the set of flowers.)
Premise 2: Some flowers fade quickly. (Only a part of the set of flowers has the property of fading quickly.)
Conclusion attempted: All roses fade quickly.

The problem lies in Premise 2. It only tells us that a subset of flowers fades quickly, but it does not tell us which flowers those are. Roses may or may not be among the flowers that fade quickly. Since the two premises leave open the possibility that roses are among the flowers that do NOT fade quickly, the conclusion does not logically follow.

For the conclusion "all roses fade quickly" to be valid, you would need a premise that directly links roses to the property of fading quickly, such as "all flowers fade quickly" (which would make Premise 2 a universal statement rather than a partial one).

In summary, the argument commits the fallacy of drawing a universal conclusion from a particular (partial) premise. The most we could validly say, given these two premises alone, is: "Some flowers fade quickly, and roses are flowers" — which still tells us nothing definitive about whether roses specifically fade quickly.

This is not a factual question, so it does not require a Wikipedia search, and it is not the kind of question I can answer definitively — because there is no single "best" programming language. The answer depends entirely on your goals, context, and needs. Here are some common considerations:

Purpose matters most. Different languages excel in different areas. For example, Python is widely favored for data science, machine learning, and scripting. JavaScript is dominant in web development. C and C++ are preferred for systems programming and performance-critical applications. Java and C# are common in enterprise software. Swift and Kotlin are used for iOS and Android development, respectively. SQL is essential for database work.

Ease of learning. If you are a beginner, languages like Python or JavaScript are often recommended because of their readable syntax and large communities.

Performance. If raw speed and memory control are priorities, C, C++, or Rust are strong choices.

Community and ecosystem. A language with a large, active community means more libraries, frameworks, tutorials, and job opportunities.

Job market. Languages like Python, JavaScript, Java, and SQL are consistently in high demand by employers.

In short, the "best" language is the one that best fits what you are trying to build and where you are in your learning journey. There is no universal answer, and experienced developers typically know several languages and choose the right tool for each task.

Great question! Here is a summary of what I can do:

**Answer Factual Questions**
I can look up information about people, places, events, dates, numbers, definitions, history, science, geography, and much more — all grounded in Wikipedia. I search in real time and base my answers on what I actually find, so you can trust the information is sourced.

**Handle Multi-Step Research**
For complex questions that require chaining multiple facts together (e.g., "Who was the president of France when the Eiffel Tower was built, and what else happened that year?"), I can search step by step and combine the results into a coherent answer.

**Clarify Ambiguous Topics**
If your question could refer to more than one thing (like "Mercury" meaning a planet, an element, or a Roman god), I will identify the most likely meaning and note the alternatives.

**Answer Non-Factual Questions Directly**
For things like arithmetic, logic puzzles, language translation, or questions about me, I answer directly without needing to search — and I will tell you when I am doing that.

**What I Do NOT Do**
I do not answer from my own memory for factual questions — I always search Wikipedia first. If I cannot find something on Wikipedia, I will tell you plainly rather than guess or make something up. I also do not browse the general web, access real-time news, or use sources outside of Wikipedia.

In short, think of me as a careful, Wikipedia-powered research assistant. Ask me anything factual and I will look it up honestly and accurately!
